 ‘The Debt Is Not the Problem’: Ramsey Host to Stay-at-Home Mom of 7 Who Borrowed Student Loans for Groceries
 A stay-at-home mom of seven called a debt show for help paying off her student loans and credit cards, and the host told her the debt was the least of her problems.
 By Jake FitzGerald 
 Published November 3, 2026, 5:38am ET · 4 min read 
 Money Talks desk. Editor: Jake FitzGerald .
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 George Kamel told Melody her marriage and financial safety were the real crisis, not the debt itself.
 Melody's student loans at 7% were actually cheaper than credit cards averaging 21% APR, making them her least harmful option.
 Without access to household income, no debt payoff plan works. Financial access must come before any debt snowball attempt.

 George Kamel was handed a debt question and declined to give a debt answer. On the October 27, 2026 episode of The Ramsey Show , a stay-at-home mom of seven in Flint, Michigan, named Melody called in. The show’s own episode description described her call as a payoff problem: “My husband says he is not a bank and he will not pay all our bills. How do I even begin to pay off debt?” 
 Kamel, a Ramsey Solutions personality, replied: “At this point, the Ramsey plan can only exist when you have some financial footing. And right now, you’re in a much bigger storm. And so right now, the debt is not the problem. The problem is: is this marriage going to survive? And what’s it going to look like if it doesn’t?” 
 If you run a debt payoff plan in a household where someone else controls the income, your effort creates more debt.
 How Groceries Ended Up on Student Loans
 Melody said she went back to school from home while her kids were young. Her husband “still expected me to contribute financially to the household,” including groceries, Christmas and birthdays. “I had to take out student loans just to be able to survive,” she said. Groceries went on credit cards.
 He covered the mortgage and utilities, she said, and bought “a boat, he’s bought a four-wheeler, he’s bought a motorcycle.” When she asked for money, he told her “I’m not a bank. I’ll give you a loan if you need it.” She said he calls her bad with money and ungrateful.
 Kamel Made the Right Call, and the Math Shows Why
 Kamel is correct. The debt snowball (pay minimums on everything, put every extra dollar at the smallest balance) runs on one fuel: monthly surplus. A caller with no income of her own has nothing to put.
 Take an simple example. Say a family of nine puts a conservative $800 a month of groceries on a card. After a year, that balance hits $9,600.
 Card APRs average 21%, sitting in record territory. Carrying that balance costs about $2,034 a year in interest. At the 7% federal rate for new college loans this school year, the same amount costs about $626. Taking out student loans for food sounds reckless, but it was the cheaper of her two lifelines.
 Now try the snowball. Say she scrapes up $300 a month for the card while groceries keep piling on. The balance still grows $500 a month before interest, or $6,000 a year. Each payment is buried by next month’s grocery bill. With prices up 4% from a year ago, that bill continues going up.
 One Variable Flips the Outcome: Who Controls the Cash
 Change a single input. If household income covers the grocery bill, the same $300 a month clears the balance in about 48 months. Total interest comes to roughly $4,669. That hurts, but it ends. Without access to the money, there is no payoff date.
 That is why Rachel Cruze’s prescription targeted access before any debt plan. “I would find a good therapist,” she said, plus hard boundaries: “I’m going to have access to the checking account and I will sit down and we can do a budget together.” 
 Cruze chose her words carefully: “I’m always careful when we throw around words like infidelity or abuse.” She described “a level of power play where he has the power and the control,” adding, “George and I can’t set that for you.” Kamel closed with: “You gotta protect your kids, protect yourself. And I would find someone safe that you can confide in and maybe stay with for a while.” 
 Steps to Take Before Starting Any Debt Snowball
 Ten days earlier, Clark Howard described Ramsey’s role this way: “Dave is more a firefighter, he’s dealing with people whose financial life is on fire.” This call shows where even the firefighter hands off. If your situation looks like Melody’s, start here:
 Map who controls each dollar. List every household income source, which account it lands in, and who can withdraw from it. If you can’t name a dollar you control, any debt plan you write will fail.
 Rank your debts by APR. Write down each balance and its rate. Cards near 21% cost far more than federal loans near 7%, so if you are forced to taking out, the cheaper debt does less damage.
 Get your credit reports. AnnualCreditReport.com shows every account in your name, including any you didn’t open yourself.
 Check your federal loan options. StudentAid.gov’s Loan Simulator shows what payment plans your actual income qualifies for. With little or no income, an income-based payment can continues the loans from adding to the crisis.
 Line up a safe person and a place to stay. Kamel’s advice counts as a financial step too: a fallback place to live sets a ceiling on how bad things can get.
 Once that foundation exists, the snowball can finally start doing its job.
